ai_summary:
Great Britain’s wind output currently stands at 13.9 GW, with estimated Scottish wind output reaching 2.2 GW, representing 21.8% of installed Scottish wind capacity. This robust generation has driven Scottish carbon intensity down to 0 gCO2/kWh, standing in stark contrast to the GB-wide figure of 115 gCO2/kWh. However, transmission bottlenecks continue to limit power transfers across the border, forcing system operators to actively curtail local supply. 

Scottish generation curtailed so far today stands at 36.9 GWh, accumulating a constraint cost of about £969,202. To compensate for this turned-down zero-carbon electricity, thermal units were dispatched elsewhere on the network, leading to an estimated 7,012,273 m3 of gas burned and releasing 12,917 tonnes of additional CO2. 

Annualising today’s constraint spending indicates an estimated yearly curtailment cost of £354 million. Spread across national demand, these recurring network balancing actions add an estimated £1/MWh to electricity invoices for consumers across the UK. Resolving these structural grid constraints remains critical to reducing consumer exposure to balancing costs and fully realising the emissions-reduction benefits of Scotland's renewable fleet.
